newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo says wants to be president of Argentina.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo says wants to be president of Argentina.

text.p: Argentina's former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo announced he wants to be president and will stand in next year's legislative elections as a first step.

But Cavallo said in a news conference in his native province of Cordoba late Monday night that he still did not know if he will be ready to launch his bid to lead the nation by the next presidential elections in 1999.
"I don't know if my time will come in 1999, 2003 or in 2007. Think that I am 50 years old, so I have plenty of time for politics ahead of me," he said.
Cavallo, who was sacked by President Carlos Menem in August, said he would continue to support Menem but would not be joining his Peronist (Justicialista) Party.

"I am not a Justicialista and it would not make any sense for me to be joining now...I am going to look for my my place among those who without being Peronists have supported this transformation of the economy and foreign policy which President Menem has led and continues to lead."
Cavallo, who will run for the lower house of Congress, named dissident former Peronist Interior Minister Gustavo Beliz as a likely political ally.

He said Menem was being misled by members of his entourage "who whisper into his ear and call themselves his friends, who have tried to use him to do business for themselves or have done corrupt business."

But he said the economy -- now under the control of former Central Bank President Roque Fernandez -- was developing smoothly: "The everyday management of the economy is being carried out as if it were on automatic pilot. And it is very good for the economy to be on automatic piot."

Cavallo is seen as the architect of Argentina's sweeping economic changes since 1991, when he launched the "Convertibility Plan" pegging the peso at par with the dollar which has almost completely stamped out inflation.

Cavallo's fall from favor with Menem came after a long series of clashes with traditionalist Peronists opposed to his free market policies, and also spectacular accusations of official corruption made by the minister.

Earlier in the day, before declaring he wanted to be president, Cavallo formally retracted accusations of corruption he made against a federal judge. Judge Augusto Belluscio had started legal proceedings against him.
